source.title: COSMOS: Predictable and Cost-Effective Adaptation of LLMs
source.authors: Jiayu Wang; Aws Albarghouthi; Frederic Sala

page_placements.theme: Context length and prompting have their own conditional scaling curves

record.tranche_reason: Uses a low-sample scaling-law predictor for retrieval-augmented ICL performance, but does not test the cited pretraining loss scaling laws or their compute-optimal allocation claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scaling-related results for retrieval-augmented ICL, which are recorded as findings not covered by the claim versions. Its QLoRA adaptation, routing, and overall COSMOS results do not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy or the claimed parameter/token/compute relationships. Citations to Kaplan and Hoffmann are background, not results from this study.
record.test_reason: The study builds a cost/performance predictor for adapting fixed pretrained LLMs (QLoRA, retrieval-augmented ICL) and reports only the predictor's accuracy and cost savings. Its 'scaling law' is an exponential saturation curve over ICL shot count, not a power law in parameters, tokens or compute. It reports no pretraining loss, no model-size sweep tied to scale, and no downstream prediction from scale or pretraining loss. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as background.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that COSMOS predicts performance and cost of adaptation strategies cheaply and accurately: 1.09% MAE for optimal-strategy accuracy and 92.72% average cost reduction. It does so using an embedding-based linear proxy for QLoRA and a low-sample saturation-curve predictor for retrieval-augmented ICL.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an exponential saturation fit to predict retrieval-augmented ICL accuracy from shot counts, alongside a separate embedding-based fine-tuning proxy; it does not reproduce the original pretraining-loss measurements or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: The ICL predictor is fit using measurements from 1-shot and 8-shot settings; the authors set its baseline performance to the lower of zero-shot performance and 1-shot results. The text also reports a HellaSwag ICL cost-prediction outlier attributable to estimating sequence lengths from training-set averages.

fits_no_version.finding: For Llama 3 8B, retrieval-augmented ICL accuracy versus shot count follows an exponential saturation curve. Fitted on 1- and 8-shot points, it predicts the other shot counts with MAE 0.003–0.013 (average 0.0085) across eight tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-context-learning accuracy as a function of demonstration count saturates exponentially and can be extrapolated from two measurements.

record.problems: The reported ICL prediction MAEs concern downstream accuracy rather than pretraining cross-entropy. No uncertainty estimates are given alongside those task-specific MAEs, although the experiments report averaging across three seeds.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded QLoRA proxy, cost-prediction, strategy-selection, and routing results because they do not measure pretraining loss scaling or the claimed allocation relationship. Their results appear in Sections 5 and Appendices D–J.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss measured against parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large pretraining runs.
No comparison of model shape at a fixed parameter count.
No power-law fit in N, D or C for fine-tuning or other regimes. The QLoRA data-portion sweep is used only to train and score a proxy predictor.
Downstream accuracy is not related to model scale or pretraining loss. Two to five models of 2B–9B are used only as a selection pool.
No fitting-choice analysis of pretraining scaling exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The 'scaling law' here is an exponential saturation in shot count, not a power law. Appendix B also fits a power law to Together.ai pricing versus token count; this is a cost model, not a scaling result. The QLoRA and routing results are rightly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweeps over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation from small pretraining runs to much larger runs.
No compute-optimal parameter-count and token-count allocation study.
No comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
Does not test whether the claimed pretraining-loss power-law form transfers to other modalities or training regimes.
Predicts adaptation accuracy from adaptation configurations, not downstream performance from model scale or pretraining loss.
Does not examine dependence of pretraining scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices.

tranche.reason: Section 4.3 uses an empirical saturation curve as an adaptation predictor; Appendix E.3 evaluates that predictor's own accuracy.

source_check.notes: Rows r1–r8 are own-method prediction errors, not evidence for a claim version; their none links and cannot_determine states are appropriate. Appendix C.2 also specifies a curve offset chosen as the lower of zero-shot and 1-shot accuracy.
